subsection: 4. The outbreak of the Troubles: from 1969 to Direct Rule, 1972

notes.h: August 1969: Derry and Belfast erupt, and the police reforms that followed
notes.b: The Apprentice Boys' parade in Derry in August 1969 led to street fighting, and British troops were sent in to restore order.
points: On 12 August 1969 the Apprentice Boys' parade passed close to the Bogside, and stone-throwing and clashes with the RUC began.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969, and residents erected barricades that became the 'Free Derry' area.
British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969, the start of the army's long involvement in internal security.
Rioting in Belfast from 14 to 16 August 1969 saw Catholic areas such as Bombay Street burned, and several people died.
Thousands of Catholic families fled their homes in Belfast and Derry, and refugee centres were set up in the Republic and in Catholic parishes.
The events of August 1969 are often treated as the start of the Troubles in their most violent form.
The Hunt Report, published in October 1969, was led by Lord Hunt and recommended a reformed police force, the RUC, with a civilian role.
It recommended that the RUC should not be routinely armed and that the B Specials should be disbanded.
The Ulster Defence Regiment was created in 1970 as a part-time army regiment to replace the B Specials.

notes.b: The split in the IRA at the end of 1969 created the Provisional IRA, which argued that the Catholic community needed armed defence.
points: The IRA split in December 1969, with the Provisional IRA breaking away from the leadership that became the Official IRA.
The Provisionals argued that the IRA must defend Catholic areas and that British forces should be driven out, a position that gained support after August 1969.
A separate Provisional Sinn Féin was set up in 1970 to match the new military wing.
The Falls Road curfew of July 1970 saw troops search houses for weapons, and several civilians were killed during the operation.
The Social Democratic and Labour Party was founded in August 1970 by nationalist politicians including Gerry Fitt and John Hume.
The Alliance Party was founded in April 1970 as a cross-community party that drew support from both communities.

notes.b: Loyalist paramilitary groups grew in response to the republican campaign, and they attacked Catholic civilians and republicans.
points: The Ulster Volunteer Force was revived in 1966, and in the early years of the Troubles it carried out attacks on Catholic targets.
The Ulster Defence Association, a loose umbrella of loyalist groups, was formed in 1971 and grew rapidly in working-class Protestant areas.
Loyalist violence increased after internment, and loyalist killings of Catholic civilians were a feature of 1971 and 1972.
The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 people, and loyalists were responsible.
Loyalist paramilitaries claimed that their violence defended the Union, while many loyalist violence incidents were carried out by men who were not formally members of any group.

notes.h: Key personality: Brian Faulkner (part 1, as Prime Minister)
notes.b: Faulkner was the Prime Minister who introduced internment and then saw the government collapse under the pressure of violence and British policy.
points: Brian Faulkner, born in 1921, had been Minister of Commerce under O'Neill before becoming Prime Minister.
He succeeded James Chichester-Clark as Prime Minister in March 1971.
He requested the introduction of internment, which began on 9 August 1971, and he defended it as necessary to stop the IRA.
He participated in the talks with Westminster on the control of security, and he insisted that Stormont should keep its powers over policing and order.
Contemporary unionists praised his firmness on security, while nationalists saw internment as a deliberate attack on the Catholic community.
He resigned in March 1972 when Westminster took over security through Direct Rule, and historians see him as a leader who lost control of events he could not contain.

notes.h: Internment and the Ballymurphy killings, August 1971
notes.b: Internment was introduced on 9 August 1971 and was applied mainly to republicans, and the violence that followed killed civilians.
points: Internment, the detention of suspects without trial, began on 9 August 1971 in an operation that arrested hundreds of people in the first days.
Those arrested were almost entirely Catholic, and many were republicans, while loyalist suspects were rarely interned.
Interrogation methods known as the five techniques, which included hooding and sleep deprivation, were used on internees.
The Compton inquiry and the Parker inquiry examined the interrogation methods, and the European Court of Human Rights later found the techniques to be inhuman and degrading but not torture.
Ballymurphy, in west Belfast, saw the deaths of eleven civilians during the army operations of 9 to 11 August 1971.
The internment policy was seen by nationalists as proof of bias and it drove many Catholics to support the Provisional IRA.

notes.b: A civil rights march in Derry against internment ended with British paratroopers killing thirteen civilians, an event that deepened the conflict.
points: The NICRA march of 30 January 1972 in Derry protested against internment and was banned by the authorities.
Soldiers of the 1st Battalion, Parachute Regiment, moved into the Bogside, and they fired on marchers and bystanders, killing thirteen people on the day.
A fourteenth man who was wounded later died, and many of the dead were shot in the back or while unarmed.
The Widgery Report of 10 April 1972 largely accepted the army's account, and this was widely rejected by nationalists.
The Saville Inquiry, reporting in 2010, found that the soldiers' firing was unjustified and that the dead were not armed.
The killings led to the burning of the British embassy in Dublin on 2 February 1972, and they increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA.

notes.h: Stormont suspended and Direct Rule, March 1972
notes.b: Stormont was suspended and government was taken over by Westminster after the British government refused to hand security powers to Stormont.
points: Faulkner demanded control of security from Westminster, but the British government under Edward Heath refused.
Faulkner resigned as Prime Minister on 24 March 1972, the same day Westminster suspended the Stormont parliament.
The Northern Ireland (Temporary Provisions) Act 1972 introduced Direct Rule from 30 March 1972, placing the province under a Secretary of State.
William Whitelaw was the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and governed through civil servants and the army.
Direct Rule was intended to be temporary, but it lasted until the restoration of devolution attempts in later years, because no agreed power-sharing settlement was reached.
The Stormont parliament was formally abolished in 1973 by the Northern Ireland Constitution Act.

notes.h: Bloody Friday and Operation Motorman, July 1972
notes.b: The IRA bombings of 21 July 1972 killed nine people in Belfast, and the army's Operation Motorman broke the IRA's no-go areas.
points: On 21 July 1972, the Provisional IRA set off more than twenty bombs in Belfast city centre, a day that became known as Bloody Friday.
Nine people died in the bombings, and many more were injured, and the attacks shocked public opinion in Britain and Northern Ireland.
Operation Motorman, launched on 31 July 1972, saw the army move into the no-go areas in Belfast and Derry, including the Creggan, the Bogside and Ardoyne.
The operation dismantled the barricades and restored government control over areas that the IRA had controlled.
The IRA's campaign continued after Motorman, and the army's presence became a permanent feature of life in Catholic areas.

notes.h: Why the Troubles erupted and lasted
points: Discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting gave the civil rights movement a sustained base of grievance.
The state's security forces, the B Specials and the RUC, were seen by Catholics as partisan, which turned protest into a security issue.
The Provisional IRA gave the Catholic community a military organisation, and its campaign drew the British army into the conflict.
Loyalist paramilitaries defended Protestant areas and attacked Catholic civilians, which increased the cycle of reprisal.
Internment and Bloody Sunday hardened attitudes on both sides and made political compromise harder.
Stormont's inability to share power with nationalists meant there was no political institution capable of containing the violence.

notes.h: Assessment: Direct Rule and the failure of Stormont
points: Achievement: Stormont's collapse removed a unionist-controlled institution that nationalists had rejected since 1921, and it opened the way for a new political settlement.
Failure: the Stormont government could not contain the violence, and its reliance on internment alienated the Catholic community.
Contemporary view: unionists saw the suspension of Stormont as a betrayal by Westminster, while nationalists welcomed it as the end of an unfair system.
Later view: historians argue that the 1972 settlement was forced by violence, and that the Unionist government's decline was a product of its own policies as well as republican action.
Contemporary view: the British government saw Direct Rule as a temporary measure, but it proved to be a long-term policy.

keyTerms.definition: The use of violence against civilians and the state to achieve political aims, used by both republican and loyalist paramilitaries in this period.
Hostility and violence between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance, which intensified during the early Troubles.
The government of Northern Ireland by Westminster through a Secretary of State, introduced in March 1972 after Stormont was suspended.
The detention of suspects without trial, introduced in Northern Ireland on 9 August 1971 and applied mainly to republicans.
The republican paramilitary organisation that split from the IRA in December 1969 and conducted the main republican campaign of the Troubles.
The killing of thirteen civilians by British paratroopers during a civil rights march in Derry on 30 January 1972.
The British army operation of 31 July 1972 that removed the IRA's barricades and no-go areas in Belfast and Derry.
The part-time army regiment formed in 1970 to replace the B Specials as the local security force.
